1343: Most forest monks eat one meal a day, before midday without fail.
Most forest monks eat two meals a day, in keeping with the ascetic practices.
Most forest monks eat one meal a day, taken straight from the alms bowl.
1344: Strictly keeping the ascetic practices helps scour away defilements and makes the body hardy.
Strictly keeping the ascetic practices is something only a few monks take up.
Strictly keeping the ascetic practices helps a monk live on very little indeed.
1345: Monks undertake not to eat any food from dawn until the following midday.
Monks undertake not to eat any solid food after the alms round at all.
Monks undertake not to handle money from the day they ordain.
1346: Fruit with seeds must be cut with a knife by a lay person before a monk may eat it.
Fruit with seeds must be marked with a knife while saying kappiyam bhante before a monk may eat it.
Fruit with seeds must be cut with a knife while saying kappiyam bhante before a novice may eat it.
1347: After midday a monk can't eat food, but he may drink plain water, which is always allowed.
After midday a monk can't eat food, but he may drink nam pana, the strained coconut water.
After midday a monk can't eat anything at all, not even nam pana, the strained fruit juice.
1348: In some monasteries, dark chocolate counts as allowable after midday because it isn't a meal.
In some monasteries, dark chocolate isn't allowed after midday at all.
In some monasteries, green tea counts as allowable after midday because it has medicinal value.
1349: Many Thai men ordain as monks for a time to make merit for a dead parent.
Many Thai men ordain as novices for a time to repay their parents' loving kindness.
Many Thai men ordain as monks for three months during the rains retreat.
1350: Before ordaining, a man must go and ask his parents' blessing first.
Before ordaining, a man must learn the Pali requests by heart first.
Before ordaining, a man must go and entrust himself to the abbot first.
1351: Offering sangha-dana is making merit to the Sangha as a whole, and the gift is usually everyday things.
Offering sangha-dana is making merit to one's own teacher, rather than to the Sangha at large.
Offering sangha-dana is making merit to the Sangha as a whole, not to any one particular temple.
1352: When you ask a monk whether he's eaten, you mustn't speak before he does.
When you ask a monk whether he's well, you mustn't use the word gin.
When you ask a monk a question at all, you should kneel first.
1353: If a monk is gravely ill, his disciples take him to the hospital themselves.
If a monk is gravely ill, the abbot invites a doctor to attend him.
If a monk is gravely ill, his disciples invite a doctor to the temple at once.
1354: I offer my blessings, lay friend — have you come far today?
I offer my blessings, lay friend — have you eaten yet today?
I offer my blessings, lay friend — is the family all well?
1355: I've been at this forest temple for three rains now, lay friend.

1356: I'd say try to calm your mind first, lay friend — the rest will follow in time.

I'd say try to calm your mind first, lay friend — then come and talk to me again.
1357: Reverence to you, Phra Ajahn — may I invite you to take the midday meal at our home next Sunday?
Reverence to you, Phra Ajahn — may I invite you to chant at our home this Sunday?
Reverence to you, Phra Ajahn — may I invite you to take the midday meal at the temple hall?
